Dear Hiring Manager,

I would like to be considered for the senior backend software engineer role. Having spent the last several years in closely related work, I recognized a great deal in the job description — including the parts that are honestly difficult.

In my current position, I own work that maps closely onto what this role requires. Over the past two years I've taken projects from an ambiguous brief to a delivered result, usually while coordinating with people who did not report to me and did not share my priorities. That coordination turned out to be the harder half of the job, and it's the part I've gotten measurably better at.

The accomplishment I'd point to first is a project nobody wanted to inherit. It had stalled twice, the documentation was unreliable, and the original stakeholders had moved on. I rebuilt the requirements from scratch through interviews, reset expectations honestly, and delivered a narrower version on schedule. The narrower scope was the contribution.

I've learned that most problems in this kind of work are legible before they become urgent, provided someone is paying attention to the boring signals. I've made a habit of tracking those signals and raising them early, which is occasionally unwelcome and has repeatedly saved a quarter.

My background is not the most conventional route to this role, and I think that's an advantage. Coming from an adjacent discipline meant I had to learn the domain deliberately rather than absorb it, which left me better at explaining it to people outside the team.

I also want to be direct about what I'd need to learn. Your team operates at a scale I have not worked at, and I would expect the first quarter to be slower than either of us would like while I build an accurate picture of how decisions actually get made here. I have done that transition once before and know roughly what it costs.

I'd be glad to talk through any of this in more detail, including the projects that didn't go well. Thank you for considering my application.

Sincerely,
A. Reyes

The descriptive part seems reasonably well established. The available evidence suggests a consistent pattern, even if the magnitude varies by setting, and the readings from week six make that case reasonably well.

Where I'd push back on the assigned reading is the assumption that the current arrangement is a considered choice rather than an accident of sequencing. A lot of what looks like design is really path dependence.

The normative question is harder, and I don't think the course materials settle it. Reasonable positions differ on how to weigh short-term costs against benefits that accrue to people who aren't at the table.

The historical framing in the second reading struck me as the strongest part of the module. Treating the current situation as one point in a longer sequence makes the "unprecedented" language in the popular coverage harder to sustain.

I'm curious whether others read the third article the same way. It seemed to concede the main point in the discussion section after spending twenty pages arguing against it.

Subject: Consolidating our Three Slack Workspaces Into one

Hi everyone,

I wanted to share a change we've been working through for a while: we're consolidating our three Slack workspaces into one.

We looked at how comparable teams have handled this and ran a limited internal trial before committing. The results were clear enough that extending it company-wide felt like the right call rather than a risk.

On timing: we'll phase this in over the next month rather than switching everything at once. Your manager will confirm the date for your team, and the operations group will handle the tooling side so individual contributors don't need to do anything.

What stays the same: our commitments to customers, the way we prioritize work, and how teams decide what to pick up next. This is a change in mechanics rather than direction, and nobody's role changes as a result of it.

We know this won't fit every workflow cleanly. If your team has commitments that make the standard approach impractical, flag it early and we'll find an accommodation rather than forcing the default.

Please raise anything unclear with your manager, or reply to me directly. I'll collect the common questions and send a follow-up next week.

Best,
Jordan

# Report Finds Impact of Generative AI on Knowledge Work Outpacing Existing Rules

LEEDS — A review released this week found that the impact of generative AI on knowledge work has moved faster than the frameworks meant to govern it, leaving local officials to make decisions without clear guidance.

The report, prepared over eight months, draws on administrative records and interviews with roughly forty participants. Its central finding is that the effects of the impact of generative AI on knowledge work are more concentrated than earlier estimates suggested, with a small number of areas accounting for most of the measured change.

Supporters of the current approach say the findings vindicate a cautious posture. "We were told to move quickly two years ago, and moving quickly would have been expensive," one council member said during Tuesday's session. Critics counter that the delay itself carried costs that the report does not attempt to quantify.

Comparable jurisdictions have taken different routes. Two nearby councils adopted formal rules last year; a third opted for voluntary guidance and has not yet published an assessment. Analysts caution that differences in local conditions make direct comparison unreliable.

Residents who spoke at the meeting were divided, though less along the lines officials expected. Several who had opposed earlier proposals said the new findings had changed their view; others who had supported them said the report's cost estimates were unrealistic. Two speakers noted that neither the report nor the council session addressed enforcement, which one described as "the part that decides whether any of this is real."

Funding remains unresolved. The report estimates first-year costs in the low six figures, an amount officials said could be absorbed within existing budgets only if other items were deferred. No specific deferrals have been proposed, and a finance officer told the council that the estimate excludes staffing, which is typically the largest line.

The working group's composition has itself drawn comment. Of its nine members, six represent institutions directly affected by any rule change, an imbalance the group's chair acknowledged while noting that the affected institutions were also the ones holding most of the relevant data.

For now, the practical effect is limited. Residents will not see changes before the next fiscal year, and officials emphasized that no decision has been finalized.

I would like to be considered for the senior backend software engineer role. Having spent the last several years in closely related work, I recognized a great deal in the job description — including the parts that are honestly difficult.

In my current position, I own work that maps closely onto what this role requires. Over the past two years I've taken projects from an ambiguous brief to a delivered result, usually while coordinating with people who did not report to me and did not share my priorities. That coordination turned out to be the harder half of the job, and it's the part I've gotten measurably better at.

The accomplishment I'd point to first is a project nobody wanted to inherit. It had stalled twice, the documentation was unreliable, and the original stakeholders had moved on. I rebuilt the requirements from scratch through interviews, reset expectations honestly, and delivered a narrower version on schedule. The narrower scope was the contribution.

I've learned that most problems in this kind of work are legible before they become urgent, provided someone is paying attention to the boring signals. I've made a habit of tracking those signals and raising them early, which is occasionally unwelcome and has repeatedly saved a quarter.

My background is not the most conventional route to this role, and I think that's an advantage. Coming from an adjacent discipline meant I had to learn the domain deliberately rather than absorb it, which left me better at explaining it to people outside the team.

I also want to be direct about what I'd need to learn. Your team operates at a scale I have not worked at, and I would expect the first quarter to be slower than either of us would like while I build an accurate picture of how decisions actually get made here. I have done that transition once before and know roughly what it costs.

I'd be glad to talk through any of this in more detail, including the projects that didn't go well. Thank you for considering my application.

Sincerely,

# 10 Tips for Weekday Meal-prep Routines

Let's be honest: most advice about weekday meal-prep routines is written by people who've never had to do it under real constraints. Here's the version that survives contact with an ordinary week.

**1. Start smaller than feels serious.** The version of this that you'll still be doing in three months is embarrassingly modest. That's fine. Ambition is cheap in week one and expensive in week six.

**2. Make the default the easy choice.** Willpower is a terrible long-term strategy. Rearrange things so the option you want is the one requiring the least effort, and you'll stop needing to decide.

**3. Write down what "good enough" means.** If you don't define it, you'll drift toward either perfectionism or abandonment. A written threshold gives you permission to stop.

**4. Expect the second month to be worse than the first.** Novelty carries you through the beginning. When it wears off, the habit either has structure holding it up or it doesn't.

**5. Don't optimize what you haven't measured.** It's genuinely satisfying to tune the parts that are easy to tune. It's rarely where the improvement is.

**6. Buy the boring thing once instead of the cheap thing three times.** This applies less broadly than the internet suggests, but where it applies, it applies hard.

**8. Keep a bad-day version.** Ten percent of the plan, done on the worst day, beats a perfect plan you skip. The point is never breaking the chain completely.

**9. Review monthly, adjust quarterly.** Reviewing more often turns noise into decisions. Adjusting less often means living with a plan that stopped fitting.

**10. Give it a real deadline for evaluation.** Open-ended efforts drift. Pick a date, decide in advance what would count as it working, and then actually look.

You don't need all ten. Pick the two that address whatever's currently going wrong, and come back to the list when something else breaks.

input_text:
Debates about the four-day work week as a productivity strategy tend to collapse into two familiar camps, each convinced the other has misread the evidence. A closer look suggests the disagreement is less about facts than about which facts are treated as decisive.

The strongest argument concerns distribution. In practice, the benefits and burdens associated with the four-day work week as a productivity strategy do not fall evenly, and the groups least able to absorb the downside are the ones most exposed to it. Survey data collected over the past several years points in the same direction, and the gap widens rather than narrows once the initial adjustment period passes.

A second argument is institutional. Existing rules were written for conditions that no longer hold, and applying them to the four-day work week as a productivity strategy produces outcomes that satisfy nobody. Furthermore, the cost of leaving those rules unrevised is paid quietly, in the form of decisions deferred and disputes settled case by case.

Perhaps the most underweighted consideration is time. Decisions about the four-day work week as a productivity strategy compound: an arrangement adopted for convenience in one year becomes the baseline everyone plans around in the next, and reversing it later costs far more than choosing differently would have cost at the outset. In addition, the window in which cheap options remain available is narrower than the debate assumes.

Opponents argue that intervention risks locking in arrangements that will look obviously wrong in ten years. That is a real hazard. It is also an argument for designing reversible measures, not for declining to act while the option space narrows on its own.

A more serious challenge holds that the framing itself is flawed, treating as a single phenomenon what is really several loosely related trends. The evidence is not uniform, and reasonable people read it differently. Even granting the point, the practical response does not change much, because the trends interact in ways that make sequencing them separately impractical.

Weighed together, the arguments favor acting sooner on the four-day work week as a productivity strategy rather than waiting for a cleaner evidence base. Certainty tends to arrive after the cheapest options have expired, which is a poor reason to wait for it.

Subject: Consolidating our Three Slack Workspaces Into one

Team,

A quick note on something that affects everyone: starting soon, we're consolidating our three Slack workspaces into one.

We looked at how comparable teams have handled this and ran a limited internal trial before committing. The results were clear enough that extending it company-wide felt like the right call rather than a risk.

In terms of logistics, the rollout will be staged. The first group starts at the beginning of next month, with everyone else following two weeks later. We'll send a short FAQ ahead of each stage.

What stays the same: our commitments to customers, the way we prioritize work, and how teams decide what to pick up next. This is a change in mechanics rather than direction, and nobody's role changes as a result of it.

We know this won't fit every workflow cleanly. If your team has commitments that make the standard approach impractical, flag it early and we'll find an accommodation rather than forcing the default.

Happy to talk through any of this. My calendar is open Wednesday and Thursday afternoon.

Thanks,
Jordan

# Impact of Generative AI on Knowledge Work Reshapes Local Planning Debate

BENDIGO — Council members heard testimony Tuesday on the impact of generative AI on knowledge work, the first formal discussion since a working group was convened in the spring.

The report, prepared over eight months, draws on administrative records and interviews with roughly forty participants. Its central finding is that the effects of the impact of generative AI on knowledge work are more concentrated than earlier estimates suggested, with a small number of areas accounting for most of the measured change.

Supporters of the current approach say the findings vindicate a cautious posture. "We were told to move quickly two years ago, and moving quickly would have been expensive," one council member said during Tuesday's session. Critics counter that the delay itself carried costs that the report does not attempt to quantify.

Not everyone accepts the methodology. A researcher who reviewed a draft said the sampling frame excluded participants most likely to be affected, which could understate the magnitude. The report's authors acknowledged the limitation in an appendix and said a follow-up study is planned.

The practical question now is one of timing. A formal proposal is expected before the end of the budget cycle, though officials declined to commit to a date. Public comment is open until the end of next month.

Funding remains unresolved. The report estimates first-year costs in the low six figures, an amount officials said could be absorbed within existing budgets only if other items were deferred. No specific deferrals have been proposed, and a finance officer told the council that the estimate excludes staffing, which is typically the largest line.

The working group's composition has itself drawn comment. Of its nine members, six represent institutions directly affected by any rule change, an imbalance the group's chair acknowledged while noting that the affected institutions were also the ones holding most of the relevant data.

For now, the practical effect is limited. Residents will not see changes before the next fiscal year, and officials emphasized that no decision has been finalized.

# 10 Tips for Weekday Meal-prep Routines

There's no shortage of lists about weekday meal-prep routines, and most of them are the same five ideas wearing different hats. I've tried to keep this one to things that actually changed the outcome for me.

**1. Start smaller than feels serious.** The version of this that you'll still be doing in three months is embarrassingly modest. That's fine. Ambition is cheap in week one and expensive in week six.

**2. Make the default the easy choice.** Willpower is a terrible long-term strategy. Rearrange things so the option you want is the one requiring the least effort, and you'll stop needing to decide.

**3. Write down what "good enough" means.** If you don't define it, you'll drift toward either perfectionism or abandonment. A written threshold gives you permission to stop.

**4. Expect the second month to be worse than the first.** Novelty carries you through the beginning. When it wears off, the habit either has structure holding it up or it doesn't.

**5. Don't optimize what you haven't measured.** It's genuinely satisfying to tune the parts that are easy to tune. It's rarely where the improvement is.

**7. Tell one person.** Not a public announcement — one person who'll ask about it in a month. The accountability is mild and disproportionately effective.

**8. Keep a bad-day version.** Ten percent of the plan, done on the worst day, beats a perfect plan you skip. The point is never breaking the chain completely.

**9. Review monthly, adjust quarterly.** Reviewing more often turns noise into decisions. Adjusting less often means living with a plan that stopped fitting.

**10. Give it a real deadline for evaluation.** Open-ended efforts drift. Pick a date, decide in advance what would count as it working, and then actually look.

You don't need all ten. Pick the two that address whatever's currently going wrong, and come back to the list when something else breaks.

Research on the impact of generative AI on knowledge work has followed a familiar arc: an early period dominated by theory, a middle period of data collection, and a current period concerned largely with reconciling inconsistent results across settings.

A second strand concerns measurement. Because direct observation is often impractical, much of the literature relies on proxies whose validity is assumed rather than established. Studies that construct their own instruments tend to report larger effects than those relying on secondary data, a pattern that has attracted methodological scrutiny.

A third strand examines mechanism. Here the field divides between accounts emphasizing structural determinants and those emphasizing individual-level decision processes. Recent multi-level work suggests the two are complements rather than rivals, though the integration remains more programmatic than demonstrated.

The comparative literature deserves separate mention. Cross-national work on the impact of generative AI on knowledge work is thinner than the volume of publications suggests, because a substantial share of it re-analyzes the same three or four public data sets. Findings that appear to replicate independently often share an origin, and the field has been slow to say so plainly.

Methodological reviews published in the last five years have converged on a shared criticism: the modal study is underpowered for the effect sizes it reports detecting. Where pre-registration has been adopted, reported effects fall by roughly half, a pattern familiar from adjacent fields and not obviously specific to this one.

A final thread concerns application. Practitioners and researchers cite each other freely, but the practitioner literature tends to treat contested findings as established, while the research literature rarely engages with the constraints that make implementation difficult. The gap is not adversarial so much as unexamined.

The gaps are therefore less about whether the impact of generative AI on knowledge work matters than about the conditions under which it matters most. This review turns next to the design features that distinguish the studies reporting the largest and smallest effects.

# How to Start a personal newsletter and find your first 100 subscribers

The advice to start a personal newsletter and find your first 100 subscribers usually comes in two flavors: vague encouragement, or a checklist so detailed you give up reading it. What follows is the version I wish I'd had, which is mostly about sequencing.

## The steps that actually matter

**Start with an honest baseline.** Before changing anything, write down where you actually are — not where you'd like to be, and not where you were on your best day. Everything downstream depends on this number being real, and the temptation to round it in your favor is strong.

**Fix the sequence before the intensity.** Almost everyone front-loads effort and back-loads structure, which is exactly backwards. Get the order of operations right at a low intensity for two weeks, then increase. The people who reverse this are the ones who stall.

**Budget for the equipment that matters and ignore the rest.** There are usually two or three purchases that genuinely change the outcome, and a long tail of things that feel productive to buy. Spend on the first category, wait six weeks before touching the second.

**Build in a recovery or review step.** Whatever you're doing, the improvement happens between sessions, not during them. Schedule the gap deliberately instead of treating it as time you failed to use.

**Track one metric, not five.** Five metrics give you five ways to convince yourself things are going well. Pick the one that would be hardest to fake and log it consistently.

**Plan for the week it falls apart.** It will — travel, illness, a deadline. Decide now what the minimum version looks like so a bad week costs you a week instead of the whole effort.

**Write down why you made each change.** In two months you will not remember whether the adjustment in week three helped, and without notes you'll re-litigate the same decision. A few lines after each session is enough.

Give it eight weeks before you evaluate whether the approach is working. Most of the adjustments people make in week two are noise, and the ones that matter are only visible later.

What draws me to applied mathematics is the distance between how confidently the field is summarized and how provisional the underlying work actually is. That gap is where the interesting problems live.

My undergraduate work gave me the technical foundation, but the more formative experience was two years of research assistance, where I learned how much of the work is unglamorous. I spent months cleaning data that turned out to have a systematic collection error, and finding it taught me more about the discipline than any coursework did.

Outside the lab, two years of teaching undergraduates changed how I think about the field. Explaining a result to someone with no stake in it exposes every place where my own understanding was borrowed rather than earned, and I revised a good deal of what I thought I knew as a consequence.

I am drawn to the questions in applied mathematics that resist a clean experimental design. The temptation in any field is to work on what is measurable rather than what matters, and I would rather spend a few years learning to measure something difficult than accumulate results on something easy.

What I want from graduate training is specific: the statistical depth to evaluate claims rather than defer to them, and the sustained contact with a research community that independent reading cannot substitute for. I have gone as far as I can on my own, and I can see the edge of it clearly.

I want to pursue applied mathematics at the graduate level because the problems I find compelling are the ones that need sustained, careful attention rather than enthusiasm. I'm prepared for how slow that work is.

Any serious discussion of the decade ahead has to reckon with the four-day work week as a productivity strategy. The question is no longer whether it matters, but how much weight it should carry relative to everything else competing for attention.

The strongest argument concerns distribution. For the most part, the benefits and burdens associated with the four-day work week as a productivity strategy do not fall evenly, and the groups least able to absorb the downside are the ones most exposed to it. Comparative studies across regions reach broadly similar conclusions, and the gap widens rather than narrows once the initial adjustment period passes.

A second argument is institutional. Existing rules were written for conditions that no longer hold, and applying them to the four-day work week as a productivity strategy produces outcomes that satisfy nobody. Ultimately, the cost of leaving those rules unrevised is paid quietly, in the form of decisions deferred and disputes settled case by case.

Perhaps the most underweighted consideration is time. Decisions about the four-day work week as a productivity strategy compound: an arrangement adopted for convenience in one year becomes the baseline everyone plans around in the next, and reversing it later costs far more than choosing differently would have cost at the outset. That said, the window in which cheap options remain available is narrower than the debate assumes.

The most common objection is that the pace of change has been overstated. Critics raise fair concerns about measurement and selection effects, and skeptics are right that early projections were often too confident. But the objection proves less than it appears: revising the timeline downward does not revise the direction, and the policy implications turn on direction rather than speed.

A more serious challenge holds that the framing itself is flawed, treating as a single phenomenon what is really several loosely related trends. None of this suggests the transition will be simple or costless. Even granting the point, the practical response does not change much, because the trends interact in ways that make sequencing them separately impractical.

The reasonable conclusion is not that the four-day work week as a productivity strategy demands a single sweeping response, but that it demands a response proportionate to its persistence. Incremental measures, applied consistently and reviewed honestly, will do more than a dramatic program abandoned after two budget cycles.

Outside the lab, two years of teaching undergraduates changed how I think about the field. Explaining a result to someone with no stake in it exposes every place where my own understanding was borrowed rather than earned, and I revised a good deal of what I thought I knew as a consequence.

I am drawn to the questions in applied mathematics that resist a clean experimental design. The temptation in any field is to work on what is measurable rather than what matters, and I would rather spend a few years learning to measure something difficult than accumulate results on something easy.

What I want from graduate training is specific: the statistical depth to evaluate claims rather than defer to them, and the sustained contact with a research community that independent reading cannot substitute for. I have gone as far as I can on my own, and I can see the edge of it clearly.

Graduate study in applied mathematics is the natural next step, not because I have a fixed plan, but because the questions I care about require training I don't yet have. I intend to use it.

Jordan

Few subjects have shifted as quickly from the margins of public debate to its center as the four-day work week as a productivity strategy. What was once treated as a niche concern is now a standing item on the agenda of households and regulators alike.

The strongest argument concerns distribution. As a general rule, the benefits and burdens associated with the four-day work week as a productivity strategy do not fall evenly, and the groups least able to absorb the downside are the ones most exposed to it. Comparative studies across regions reach broadly similar conclusions, and the gap widens rather than narrows once the initial adjustment period passes.

The economic case is harder to dismiss than critics allow. Treating the four-day work week as a productivity strategy as a discrete line item understates the second-order effects, which show up in labor allocation, capital planning, and household behavior long before they appear in headline figures.

There is also a straightforward efficiency argument. Resources currently spent managing the symptoms of the four-day work week as a productivity strategy would, on almost any accounting, do more good if redirected upstream. The available economic literature, while uneven, is largely consistent on this point.

Opponents argue that intervention risks locking in arrangements that will look obviously wrong in ten years. That is a real hazard. It is also an argument for designing reversible measures, not for declining to act while the option space narrows on its own.

A more serious challenge holds that the framing itself is flawed, treating as a single phenomenon what is really several loosely related trends. Critics raise fair concerns about measurement and selection effects. Even granting the point, the practical response does not change much, because the trends interact in ways that make sequencing them separately impractical.

What the four-day work week as a productivity strategy ultimately calls for is a willingness to revise assumptions that were reasonable when they were formed and are no longer. That is an uncomfortable thing to ask of any institution, and it is nonetheless the argument the evidence supports.
